1023.title: The caliphate ends, 1924
1023.hook: the Ottoman caliphate is abolished by the new Turkish Republic
1023.howItsDone: Muslims today organize religious life through mosques, scholars, councils and national religious bodies, and they hold differing views about whether and how a caliphate should exist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muhammad Iqbal, the poet of khudi, the self that rises. Your line was: the self can rise. Did you put your line of hope where you could see it? Today, something very old comes to a stop. Day one thousand twenty-three.

The new parliament of the Turkish Republic has voted, and an office no longer exists. That night in Istanbul, the man who held it is told he must leave the country. He paints and plays music, and his title, as tradition tells it, reaches back to the first generation after the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Before dawn he and his family are taken to a train heading west, into Europe. He will not come back. Far away, in India, in Egypt, in Indonesia, Muslims read the news in their papers. Some weep. Some shrug. Some start organizing to bring it back. Today: the caliphate ends.
screen: `THE PARLIAMENT HAS VOTED.` → `A PAINTER WITH AN ANCIENT TITLE.` → `A TRAIN WEST, BEFORE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Caliph comes from the Arabic khalifa, a successor or deputy. After the Prophet's death, Sunni Muslims hold, the community chose Abu Bakr as successor; Shia Muslims hold that the Prophet had named Ali. The title passed down, through dynasties and quarrels, until it rested with the Ottoman sultans. The same root reaches back into the Qur'an itself. In Pickthall's words, when God tells the angels about Adam: "Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth." A khalifa. Over the centuries, how much real power the caliph held changed a great deal. Sometimes he ruled an empire. Sometimes the title was mostly a symbol. After the Ottoman Empire fell apart following the First World War, the new parliament in Ankara first ended the sultanate, kept a caliph without a throne for a short while, and then, once the Republic was declared, abolished the office entirely. The last caliph, Abdulmecid, went into exile. How did Muslims take it? Not in one way. In India, a movement had already campaigned hard to protect the caliphate, and it lost its cause overnight. Some scholars gathered to talk about naming a new caliph, and nothing came of it. Others said that a Muslim's faith had never depended on one office in Istanbul. Today Muslims still differ: some hope to see a caliphate again, others organize their religious life through mosques, scholars and councils, and they argue about it openly. The Qur'an says of power, in Pickthall's words: "Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt." An institution ends. Prayer goes on.
screen: `KHALIFA: A SUCCESSOR, A DEPUTY.` · `FROM EMPIRE TO SYMBOL.` · `THE REPUBLIC ABOLISHES THE OFFICE.` · `MUSLIMS ANSWER IN MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `THOU WITHDRAWEST SOVEREIGNTY FROM WHOM THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about institutions ending. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one institution you once counted on that has changed or disappeared. A school that closed. A shop that held your street together. A newspaper, a club, a congregation that merged, a tradition your family stopped keeping. Notice what it held for people, and who picked up that work when it was gone, or whether no one did. If you pray, you can hold Qur'an 3:26 in mind, that sovereignty is given and withdrawn. If not, just breathe and let the place come back to you. The bell holds the time.
Khalifa. The title of the caliph, successor to the Prophet, whose office the new Turkish Republic abolished in nineteen twenty-four, sending the last caliph into exile. Today's word.
Your line: an institution ends. Today, thank someone who keeps a small institution going, a club, a mosque, a library desk, while it's still there. Day one thousand twenty-three.

1024.title: Partition, 1947
1024.hook: India and Pakistan divide, millions are displaced and many killed on all sides
1024.howItsDone: Families in Pakistan, India and Bangladesh pass down Partition memories, and Muslims, like their neighbors, remember those who died with prayers and with the words of Qur'an 2:156 said at any loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the caliphate ended, an office voted out of existence and a caliph sent west on a train. Your line was: an institution ends. Whom did you thank for keeping something going? Today is a heavy day. Go gently. Day one thousand twenty-four.

A key. An old iron house key, kept in a drawer in Lahore, or in Delhi, or in Amritsar, or in Dhaka. The family that keeps it has not seen the door it opens for generations. The grandmother who carried it out locked the house behind her, sure she'd be back in a few weeks, once things calmed down. Families on both sides of a new border keep keys like this. Hindu families, Sikh families, Muslim families. The same drawer, the same key, the same door they never opened again. Today: Partition.
screen: `AN OLD IRON KEY IN A DRAWER.` → `SURE SHE'D BE BACK IN A FEW WEEKS.` → `THE SAME KEY ON BOTH SIDES.`

segments.voice: When British rule in India ended, the land was divided into two states, India and Pakistan, with Pakistan itself in two wings, west and east. The line was drawn by a British commission in a hurry, through the provinces of Punjab and Bengal, through farms and villages and families. Some people learned which country they lived in only after independence had already come. Then came the leaving. Muslims moving toward Pakistan. Hindus and Sikhs moving toward India. On foot, in carts, on overcrowded trains. And then came the killing, done by people of every community to people of every community, neighbors turned against neighbors. Women suffered terribly. Accounts tell of trains that arrived carrying only the dead. Any honest telling has to say it plainly: there was cruelty on all sides, and grief on all sides. And there's the other thread. The oral histories gathered since include people who hid a neighbor of another faith in a grain store, walked a family to safety, refused to give up a name. Hindus sheltering Muslims. Muslims sheltering Sikhs. Sikhs sheltering Hindus. The Qur'an sets the weight of one life in a single sentence. In Pickthall's words: "whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind." Muslims say at any loss the words of surah al-Baqarah: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." In that summer, some had nothing else left to say. Grief on every side.
screen: `A LINE DRAWN IN A HURRY.` · `THE LEAVING, THEN THE KILLING.` · `NEIGHBORS WHO HID NEIGHBORS.` · `THE WEIGHT OF ONE LIFE.` · then, large: `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

segments.voice: The practice: remember all who were uprooted. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the families who left their homes in that summer. Muslim, Hindu, Sikh, Christian, and others. The ones who arrived, and the ones who didn't. The ones who hid a neighbor. The ones still holding the key. Don't sort them into sides. Just hold them, all together. If you pray, you can pray for all who were uprooted, and you can say the words Muslims say at a loss: we are Allah's, and unto Him we are returning. If not, just remember them as you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Partition. The division of British India into India and Pakistan, a leaving and a killing that left grief in every community. Today's word.
Your line: grief on every side. Today, listen to or read one Partition memory from a community other than the one you'd expect, all the way through. Day one thousand twenty-four.

1025.title: Independence movements
1025.hook: from Indonesia to Algeria, Muslim-majority lands gain independence, often at great cost
1025.howItsDone: Muslim-majority countries mark their independence days with flags, speeches and remembrance of those who died, and in some of them prayers for the nation are offered in mosques on that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Partition, and the key kept in a drawer on both sides of the border. Your line was: grief on every side. Whose memory did you listen to? Today, the long walk out from under empire. Day one thousand twenty-five.

A few typed sentences, read aloud in front of a house in Jakarta to a small crowd. Two men put their names to it: Sukarno and Hatta. It says, in a few plain sentences, that the people of Indonesia declare their independence. That's it. No army behind it strong enough to hold it yet. The Dutch did not accept those sentences, and years of fighting and talks followed before they did. Across the Muslim world, the same story played out in many forms: a declaration, a cost, a flag. Today: independence movements.
screen: `A TYPED STATEMENT IN JAKARTA.` → `READ ALOUD TO A SMALL CROWD.` → `YEARS BEFORE IT HELD.`

segments.voice: Arabic has a word for it: istiqlal, independence. In Jakarta, the great national mosque was given that name: the Istiqlal Mosque, the Independence Mosque. A house of prayer named for a political freedom. The name ties the two together. Faith fed these movements in different ways. In Algeria, under French rule, the scholar Abdelhamid Ben Badis and his association of Muslim scholars opened schools to teach Arabic and the Qur'an, and a motto attributed to him put it in three short lines: Islam is my religion, Arabic is my language, Algeria is my homeland. When Algeria's war of independence came, it was long and terribly costly, on every side, and the scars are still being talked through on both shores of the Mediterranean. Not every road was war. Some lands won independence mostly through negotiation and politics. Some through uprising. Others through a mix of both. And some of the leaders were not religious figures at all. Muslims of every kind, devout, secular and in between, marched under the same flags, alongside Christian, Hindu and other neighbors. The Qur'an has a line about peoples and nations that some readers turn to here. In Pickthall's words: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." In this verse, nations are made so that they may know one another. Freedom at a cost.
screen: `ISTIQLAL: INDEPENDENCE.` · `A MOSQUE NAMED INDEPENDENCE.` · `ALGERIA: SCHOOLS, THEN A COSTLY WAR.` · `NOT EVERY ROAD WAS WAR.` · then, large: `NATIONS AND TRIBES THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn about one independence day, starting by choosing it now. Settle, and breathe. Pick one Muslim-majority country. Indonesia, Algeria, Pakistan, Morocco, Malaysia, Senegal, or another that comes to mind. Picture its flag going up for the first time. Then picture the people who weren't there to see it, the ones it cost. Hold both in the same breath, the flag and the cost. If you pray, you can remember the people of that land. If not, simply breathe with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Independence movements. The struggles that brought Muslim-majority lands out from under empire, through talks, through war, and often at great cost. Today's word.
Your line: freedom at a cost. Today, look up the independence day of the country you chose, and read who declared it and what came next. Day one thousand twenty-five.

1026.title: Enslaved African Muslims
1026.hook: many enslaved Africans brought to the Americas were Muslim, like Omar ibn Said, who wrote in Arabic
1026.howItsDone: Muslim communities in the Americas, especially African American Muslims, remember enslaved Muslims like Omar ibn Said and Bilali Muhammad in study circles, lectures and museum visits, and some mosques are named in their honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, independence movements, istiqlal, won through talks and through war. Your line was: freedom at a cost. Which independence day did you look up? Today, people who had no freedom at all, and kept their prayers anyway. Day one thousand twenty-six.

Marks on the wall of a small jail in North Carolina. A runaway has been locked up, a stranger who speaks no English anyone can follow. On the wall of his cell, people see marks they can't read: lines of flowing script, written in charcoal. Townspeople come to stare. The man is a scholar from West Africa, and the script is Arabic. He has been carried across an ocean, sold, and has run from a cruel master, and still he writes. His name is Omar ibn Said, and his story opens a chapter of American history that is easy to miss. Today: enslaved African Muslims.
screen: `A STRANGER IN A CAROLINA JAIL.` → `FLOWING SCRIPT ON THE WALL.` → `A SCHOLAR FROM WEST AFRICA.`

segments.voice: Among the Africans carried across the Atlantic in the slave trade were Muslims. Some of them were scholars, teachers and pilgrims, people who could read and write Arabic, who had memorized long stretches of the Qur'an, and who kept the daily prayers. They arrived in chains in the Caribbean, in Brazil, in the American South, and their enslavers often had no idea what the marks on a scrap of paper meant. Omar ibn Said came from Futa Toro in West Africa, where he had studied for years. In America he was enslaved, ran away, was jailed, and was then held by a family in North Carolina for the rest of his life. Years later he wrote a short account of himself, in Arabic. And how does he begin? Not with his own name. After calling on the name of God, he writes out a surah of the Qur'an, al-Mulk, the Dominion. Its first line, in Pickthall's words: "Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty, and, He is Able to do all things." Consider who is writing that. A man owned by another man, opening his life story by saying that the true sovereignty belongs to God. His enslavers later presented him as a Christian convert, and he did write Christian texts too. But he kept writing the Qur'an's words, and scholars still debate what he believed in his own heart. On the Georgia coast, another enslaved Muslim, Bilali Muhammad, left behind pages of Arabic writing on prayer and law. Men like these wrote Arabic from memory, far from any teacher, and kept the times of prayer. They prayed in chains.
screen: `MUSLIMS IN THE SLAVE SHIPS.` · `OMAR IBN SAID OF FUTA TORO.` · `HIS STORY OPENS WITH AL-MULK.` · `WHAT HE BELIEVED: STILL DEBATED.` · then, large: `IN WHOSE HAND IS THE SOVEREIGNTY.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn Omar ibn Said's story, starting with sitting beside it now. Settle, and breathe. Picture the jail wall and the charcoal script. Picture an old man at a table, years later, writing in a language no one around him can read. Let one detail stay with you: the first words he chose. If you pray, you can remember Omar and all who were enslaved, and the prayers they kept in secret. If not, just keep them company in your mind for these breaths. The bell holds the time.
Al-Mulk, the surah on God's sovereignty that Omar ibn Said wrote out from memory to open his own account of an enslaved life. Today's word.
Your line: they prayed in chains. Today, look up Omar ibn Said's own account, and read the opening he chose. Day one thousand twenty-six.

1027.title: Muslims in Britain
1027.hook: a dome in Woking, a terraced house in Liverpool, sailors by the docks in Cardiff
1027.howItsDone: British Muslims pray in a wide range of buildings, from purpose-built mosques to converted houses, shops and chapels, and some local mosques keep and share the history of the people who founded them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, enslaved African Muslims, people like Omar ibn Said who kept their faith far from home and wrote it down in Arabic, opening with al-Mulk. Your line was: they prayed in chains. Whose name did you carry with you? Day one thousand twenty-seven.

A domed mosque sits behind the trees in Woking, a quiet commuter town south of London. It is named for a woman far away, Shah Jahan, the Begum of Bhopal in India, who helped pay for it. Up north in Liverpool, a local solicitor named William Quilliam becomes Muslim, takes the name Abdullah, and opens a mosque in a row of ordinary terraced houses. Down in Cardiff, near the docks, sailors from Yemen and Somalia rent rooms, marry, raise children, and set aside a room to pray. No palace in any of it. Just streets, rain and neighbors. Today: Muslims in Britain.
screen: `A DOME IN WOKING.` → `A TERRACED HOUSE IN LIVERPOOL.` → `SAILORS BY THE CARDIFF DOCKS.`

segments.voice: Here is the one idea for today: Muslims in Britain are not a single arrival. They are many threads, woven over a long time. Some threads are converts, like Abdullah Quilliam in Liverpool. Some are sailors and dock workers, from Yemen, Somalia and the Indian subcontinent, who settled in port towns. Some are soldiers from India who fought in Britain's wars; near that mosque in Woking there is a burial ground made for Muslim soldiers. And then came families, from Pakistan, Bangladesh, India and later from Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, who came to work in mills, factories, hospitals and buses, and stayed. You can read that history in the buildings. Some mosques were built from the ground up with domes and minarets. Others began as a front room, a shop, a warehouse or an old chapel. On Brick Lane in East London stands a building that was put up as a chapel for French Protestant refugees, later served as a synagogue for Jewish families, and is now a mosque. One building, three faiths, each praying in turn under the same roof. The Qur'an has a line that fits a faith carried to a cold, rainy island: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." For British Muslims, that has meant praying in a Cardiff boarding house, a Bradford mill, a Woking garden. The faith did not wait for the perfect place. It found a corner, faced Mecca, and began.
screen: `NOT ONE ARRIVAL, MANY THREADS.` · `CONVERTS, SAILORS, SOLDIERS, FAMILIES.` · `ONE BUILDING, THREE FAITHS.` · `EAST AND WEST BELONG TO GOD.` · then, large: `A LONG BRITISH STORY.`

segments.voice: The practice: get to know your local mosque's history, starting with what you already know. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the mosque nearest where you live, or one you pass on the way to work. What was the building before? Who prayed there first? How did they find the money, the land, the patience? If you don't know, notice that, and keep the question for later. Then think of the first handful of people who unrolled their prayer mats in that place. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for them in your own words. If not, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Abdullah Quilliam, the Liverpool solicitor who became Muslim and opened one of Britain's first mosques in a row of terraced houses. Today's word.
Your line: a long british story. Today, look up one fact about the mosque nearest you: when it opened, or what the building was before. Day one thousand twenty-seven.

1028.title: Muslims in America
1028.hook: immigrants, converts and African American Muslims, a very diverse community
1028.howItsDone: American Muslims gather in mosques and Islamic centers founded by immigrant, African American and convert communities, and many mosques hold open houses where neighbors can visit and ask questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muslims in Britain: a dome in Woking, a terraced house in Liverpool where Abdullah Quilliam opened a mosque, a chapel on Brick Lane that became a mosque. Your line was: a long british story. What did you find out about the mosque nearest you? Day one thousand twenty-eight.

Friday, just after noon, in a mosque in an American city. A man in a Detroit auto plant jacket. A doctor whose parents came from Lahore. A grandmother whose family has been Black and Muslim in Philadelphia for generations. A young woman from a Lutheran family in Minnesota who became Muslim in college. A Somali taxi driver. A Bosnian baker. They stand in one row, and nobody needs to ask where anyone is really from. The answer, for all of them, is here. Today: Muslims in America.
screen: `FRIDAY, JUST AFTER NOON.` → `DETROIT, LAHORE, PHILADELPHIA, MINNESOTA.` → `WHERE ARE YOU FROM? HERE.`

segments.voice: American Muslims are a very varied community, and three big streams run into it. The first stream is immigrants. Arab families settled in the Midwest and worked in factories; South Asians came as doctors, engineers and students; later came people from Iran, Turkey, Bosnia, Somalia and many other places. The second stream is African American Muslims. Two days ago we met enslaved Africans who prayed in chains. Slavery made that faith hard to hand down. Later, Black Americans found their way to Islam again, through several movements. Some passed through the Nation of Islam, and under Warith Deen Mohammed much of that community turned to mainstream Sunni practice. The third stream is converts of every background, who walked into a mosque one day and said the shahada. Here is the idea worth keeping. For the people in that Friday row, American and Muslim are not two halves pulling apart. They are one life. The boxer Muhammad Ali took the name, prayed, fought, joked, and was American to his fingertips. The Qur'an says plainly: "There is no compulsion in religion." In America that line can be heard twice: as a teaching of the faith, and as something close to the country's own promise that belief is free. A convert chooses. An immigrant family chooses to stay. A grandchild of the old streams chooses to keep praying.
screen: `THREE STREAMS.` · `IMMIGRANTS FROM EVERYWHERE.` · `AFRICAN AMERICAN MUSLIMS, RETURNING.` · `CONVERTS WHO CHOSE.` · then, large: `THERE IS NO COMPULSION IN RELIGION.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one American Muslim's story. Settle, and breathe. Think of an American Muslim you know of: a neighbor, a coworker, a doctor, an athlete, a poet, someone from the news. What do you actually know about their life, beyond the label? Where did their family come from, or how did they come to the faith? If no one comes to mind, notice that, and choose one name to look up later today, maybe Muhammad Ali, maybe someone in your own town. If you pray, you can ask God's blessing on that person. The bell holds the time.
Shahada, the declaration a convert speaks on becoming Muslim, one of the three streams that make up American Islam. Today's word.

1029.title: Malcolm X at Hajj
1029.hook: he writes home from Mecca of pilgrims of every color in one brotherhood
1029.howItsDone: Pilgrims on Hajj wear the same simple white garments, pray in shared rows and travel the same route together, and many Muslims speak of the pilgrimage as a lesson in the equality of believers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muslims in America: immigrants, African American Muslims and converts, three streams in one community, some sealed with the shahada. Your line was: american and muslim. Whose story did you hear? Today, one American Muslim's story. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

A tall American in two plain white cloths, the pilgrim's dress, sits down to write a letter home. He has spent years as the fiery voice of a movement in America, speaking hard words about race. Now he is in Mecca, and something in him is shifting. He has walked around the Ka'ba in a crowd from every part of the world. He has eaten from the same plate and slept on the same floor as men whose skin, he writes, ranged from the palest to the darkest. And he says he has never seen anything like it. Today: Malcolm X at Hajj.
screen: `TWO WHITE CLOTHS.` → `A LETTER HOME FROM MECCA.` → `THE SAME PLATE, THE SAME FLOOR.`

segments.voice: The man was Malcolm X, and his autobiography gives a chapter to the pilgrimage and the letters he wrote from it. He describes praying, eating and sleeping beside pilgrims of every color, and says the experience made him rethink much of what he had believed about race. He went home with a new name, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz, and a new way of talking about people. What did he see? He saw the Hajj doing what it is built to do. Every pilgrim wears the same simple cloth. Every pilgrim faces the same House. In the rows of prayer, a rich man stands by a poor one and a king could stand by a farmer, heel to heel and shoulder to shoulder. The Qur'an sets human difference beside the sky and the earth: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours." Colors and languages as signs to wonder at, not ranks to climb. A saying reported from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in his farewell sermon makes a similar point: no Arab over a non-Arab, and no one of one color over another, except by mindfulness of God. Malcolm did not live long after. But the letter stayed, and so did the picture: every color, one row.
screen: `A LETTER FROM THE PILGRIMAGE.` · `A NEW NAME: EL-HAJJ MALIK EL-SHABAZZ.` · `THE SAME CLOTH, THE SAME HOUSE.` · `LANGUAGES AND COLORS, AMONG HIS SIGNS.` · then, large: `EVERY COLOR, ONE ROW.`

segments.voice: The practice: think about one brotherhood. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a time you stood or sat side by side with people very different from you, at a stadium, a funeral, a kitchen in a crisis, a prayer hall. What made the differences go quiet for a while? Then think of one person who seems other to you: different color, country, accent or faith. Picture them on your right, shoulder to shoulder, facing the same way. If you pray, you can ask God's blessing on them. The bell holds the time.

Hajj, the pilgrimage that sent Malcolm X home with a new name after praying beside pilgrims of every color. Today's word, and the end of a week that went from the caliphate's end and partition to Britain and America.
Your line: every color, one row. Today, sit or stand next to someone you usually wouldn't, and say hello. Day one thousand twenty-nine.
